title: Command Pattern
tagline: Turn requests into first-class objects — enabling undo/redo, queuing, logging, and macro recording.

sections.content:
**Problem:** A text editor has a toolbar, a menu, and keyboard shortcuts — all of which trigger the same operations (bold, cut, paste). Hard-coding the logic in each UI element duplicates code and makes undo/redo nearly impossible. When the user presses Ctrl+Z, how does the app know what to reverse?

**Core idea:** The **Command** pattern encapsulates a request as a self-contained **object** with an `execute()` method and (optionally) an `undo()` method. The object carries everything needed to perform — or reverse — the action. This lets you: **queue** commands for later execution, **log** them to disk for replay, **stack** them in a history for undo/redo, and **decouple** the invoker (button) from the receiver (document). Every action in a text editor, every transaction in a banking system, and every job in a task queue is a Command.

sections.caption: Invoker calls execute() and pushes commands onto a history stack. undo() reverses the last command — the Invoker never knows the details.

sections.title: A Restaurant Order Slip
sections.content:
When a waiter takes your order, they write it on a **slip** and pass it to the kitchen. The slip is the **Command** — it contains everything needed: table number, items, special requests. The waiter (Invoker) doesn't cook; the chef (Receiver) doesn't talk to you. If the kitchen gets backed up, slips stack up in a **queue**. If an order is wrong, the slip tells the kitchen exactly what to reverse.

This separation is why a task queue (Bull, BullMQ, Sidekiq) works: the web server writes a job object (Command) to Redis, and a worker process reads and executes it — completely decoupled, retryable, and auditable.

**Participants:**

- **Command** — interface with `execute()` and optionally `undo()`. It stores all data needed to perform the action.
- **ConcreteCommand** — implements the interface. Holds a reference to the **Receiver** and saves enough state to reverse the action (`prevState`, `deletedText`, etc.).
- **Receiver** — the object that knows how to actually perform the work (a `Document`, a `Canvas`, a database connection). Commands delegate to it.
- **Invoker** — triggers `command.execute()` and manages the history stack. It doesn't know what the command does — just that it can `execute()` and `undo()`.
- **Client** — creates concrete commands and wires them to receivers; hands commands to the invoker.

**Undo/Redo stack:** The Invoker maintains an `undoStack`. `run(cmd)` pushes to it. `undoLast()` pops and calls `cmd.undo()`. A `redoStack` enables Ctrl+Y.

**Macros:** A `MacroCommand` holds a list of commands and calls `execute()` on each — record once, replay any number of times.

**Task queues:** Libraries like BullMQ serialize Command objects to JSON, store them in Redis, and workers deserialize and call `execute()`. Retries, delays, and priority are all managed by the queue — the Command object stays simple.

**Transactional integrity:** In database systems, a Command corresponds to a transaction. `execute()` applies changes; `undo()` rolls back. The Invoker is the transaction manager.

sequenceDiagram
    participant User
    participant Invoker
    participant BoldCmd as BoldCommand
    participant Doc as Document
    User->>Invoker: run(BoldCommand)
    Invoker->>BoldCmd: execute()
    BoldCmd->>Doc: applyBold(selection)
    Doc-->>BoldCmd: confirms
    BoldCmd-->>Invoker: done (pushed to history)
    User->>Invoker: undoLast()
    Invoker->>BoldCmd: undo()
    BoldCmd->>Doc: removeBold(prevState)
    Doc-->>BoldCmd: restored
    BoldCmd-->>Invoker: undone
sections.caption: execute() applies the action and pushes onto history. undoLast() pops and calls undo() — the document is restored to its previous state.

sections.label: Runtime
sections.explanation: Each command stores the data needed for both execute() and undo(). CommandHistory is the Invoker — it manages both stacks without knowing what any command does.

sections.label: Concept
sections.explanation: The task queue pattern: commands are serializable value objects. A worker process dequeues and executes them. toJSON() enables persistence to Redis or a database.

sections.content:
**When to use:** You need undo/redo; you need to queue, schedule, or log operations; you want to decouple UI triggers from business logic; you need transactional rollback.

**When NOT to use:** For simple function calls with no undo or queuing requirement — wrapping them in command objects adds ceremony without benefit. Don't implement Command 'just in case' undo is needed someday (YAGNI).

**Trade-off:** Each operation requires a new class/object. In large apps this creates many small classes — mitigate with factory functions or command registries.

**Real frameworks:** BullMQ/Bull job objects, event sourcing (every state change = a stored Command), Redux actions (pure command objects dispatched to reducers), database migrations (`up()`/`down()` = execute/undo).

items: **Encapsulation:** A Command object bundles the action, its parameters, and enough state to undo — making every operation self-contained and auditable.
**Undo/Redo:** The Invoker maintains a history stack; undo() reverses commands in LIFO order without the Invoker knowing any business logic.
**Queueing & async:** Commands are serializable value objects — ideal for task queues (BullMQ), event sourcing, and deferred execution.
**Decoupling:** The Invoker never imports the Receiver. A button, a keyboard shortcut, and an API endpoint can all dispatch the same Command — one implementation, many triggers.
**Redux = Command:** Redux actions dispatched to reducers are Commands. `dispatch(action)` = `invoker.run(command)`.

quiz.question: What does the Command pattern encapsulate?
options: A set of related objects into a single interface.
A request as a self-contained object with execute() and undo().
An algorithm that can be swapped at runtime.
A one-to-many notification mechanism.
quiz.explanation: Command turns requests into objects carrying all data needed to execute, undo, queue, or log the operation.

quiz.question: In the Command pattern, which participant manages the undo/redo history stack?
options: The Receiver.
The ConcreteCommand.
The Invoker.
The Client.
quiz.explanation: The Invoker pushes executed commands onto a history stack and pops/calls undo() when the user requests an undo — it knows nothing about what the commands do.

quiz.question: Why must a DeleteCommand save the deleted text before executing?
options: To satisfy the Single Responsibility Principle.
To serialize itself to JSON for the task queue.
So that undo() can re-insert the text that was removed.
To prevent the Invoker from calling execute() twice.
quiz.explanation: undo() must reverse the operation exactly. Without saving the deleted text, there is no way to restore the document to its previous state.

quiz.question: How does the Command pattern relate to Redux actions?
options: Redux actions are Receivers; reducers are Commands.
Redux actions are Command objects dispatched to reducers (Invoker-like); dispatch() = run(command).
Redux uses the Observer pattern, not Command.
Redux actions cannot be undone, so the analogy does not apply.
quiz.explanation: Redux actions are plain objects (Commands) dispatched to the store. The store applies the reducer (Receiver logic) and maintains state history — a direct Command pattern application.

quiz.question: What is a MacroCommand?
options: A command that runs on a cron schedule.
A command that holds a list of commands and calls execute() on each in sequence.
A command that executes in a separate worker thread.
A command with a timeout for undo.
quiz.explanation: MacroCommand composes multiple commands. execute() iterates and runs each; undo() reverses them in reverse order — enabling recorded macro playback.

quiz.question: Why do task queues like BullMQ benefit from the Command pattern?
options: Commands are stateless, so they require no serialization.
Commands are serializable value objects that can be stored in Redis and executed by any worker.
Commands auto-retry by implementing the Observer pattern.
The Invoker in BullMQ runs inside the browser.
quiz.explanation: A job in BullMQ is a Command: its payload is stored in Redis, any worker can deserialize and execute it, and failures can be retried — decoupled producer/consumer.

quiz.question: What happens to the redo stack when a new command is executed?
options: The redo stack is merged with the undo stack.
The redo stack is cleared, because the new action forks the history.
The redo stack grows by one.
Nothing — redo is unaffected by new commands.
quiz.explanation: Executing a new command after an undo forks history. The redo branch is discarded — like a text editor clearing Ctrl+Y options after you type new characters.

quiz.question: What is the role of the Receiver in the Command pattern?
options: To maintain the list of observers.
To provide the actual implementation of the business operation that ConcreteCommands delegate to.
To serialize commands to JSON.
To decide which strategy algorithm to apply.
quiz.explanation: The Receiver knows how to perform the work (Document.insert(), Canvas.drawShape()). Commands call the Receiver — keeping the two concerns separate.

quiz.question: How does database migration (up/down) relate to the Command pattern?
options: Migrations are Observers that react to schema changes.
up() = execute(), down() = undo() — each migration is a Command applied or reversed by the migration runner (Invoker).
Migrations use the Singleton pattern to avoid duplicate schemas.
The database is the Strategy; migrations are Contexts.
quiz.explanation: Each migration file is a Command. The migration runner (Invoker) calls up() to apply or down() to roll back — textbook Command with undo.

quiz.question: When should you NOT use the Command pattern?
options: When operations need to be logged for auditing.
When undo/redo functionality is required.
When a simple function call has no queuing, logging, or undo requirement.
When multiple UI elements trigger the same operation.
quiz.explanation: YAGNI — wrapping a simple, fire-and-forget call in a Command object adds overhead and classes with no benefit. Introduce the pattern when a concrete need (undo, queue) arises.
